structure.title: Mowgli’s Brothers – “Tiger! Tiger!” · Three stories of Mowgli
structure.text: A wolf's den and a meeting of the pack come before the boy has words of his own. A bear, a panther and eventually humans offer competing educations. Each place that might take him in has rules about what counts as a member and who may speak for a cub.

structure.title: The White Seal – Toomai of the Elephants · A seal, a mongoose and an elephant keeper's son
structure.text: The collection moves out to sea, into a bungalow garden and along an elephant trail. What looked like common sense among wolves would be poor equipment for a seal seeking a safe beach. Each story begins the work of discovering a habitat afresh.

structure.title: Her Majesty’s Servants · A night among the army animals
structure.text: In the closing story the animals of a military camp discuss the orders they obey and the work they fear. Heard from among the mules, bullocks and horses, a splendid parade is an achievement made out of quite particular feet, loads and nerves.

people.name: Mowgli
people.role: Human child in a wolf pack
people.text: He learns the animals' calls and the terms under which they will come to his aid. His human skills can be an advantage among animals, but entering a human village does not make him competent in its customs.

people.name: Baloo and Bagheera
people.text: Baloo knows the words a young hunter must learn to stay alive. Bagheera remembers captivity among men. Both care for Mowgli, but when a lesson goes badly their different accounts of what the child needs become sharply audible.

context.title: The Law of the Jungle
context.text: Here the phrase can mean rules restraining violence. Adoption, access to water and the right to hunt all involve obligations. The monkeys' boast that they are exceptionally free sounds rather different when somebody needs them to keep a promise.

notice.text: Listen to the verse at the edge of a story.
notice.why: A song can give a hunter's boast, a lullaby or a working animal's rhythm the first or last word. For a moment a whole community gets to describe the world in the sounds it knows best.

notice.text: Ask what this creature can smell or hear in time.
notice.why: A flicker in the grass matters differently to a mongoose and to a human child. Suspense often begins with the time it takes the slower observer to recognise what the quicker one already knows.

opening: Mowgli grows up among wolves, learning rules that can keep him alive among creatures capable of killing him. Belonging requires more than affection: the jungle has debts, councils, enemies, and punishments, and the tiger has never accepted his place in it. Around Mowgli's adventures, Kipling tells other stories of animals facing danger with courage, cunning, and unlikely allies. The pleasure comes from entering societies with their own customs and voices, where a human child may need considerable education before he can behave intelligently.
